parts.title: My grandmother's camera
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
When my grandmother died last spring, my mother gave me her old camera. It is a heavy metal one from the 1970s, and at first I did not know what to do with it. It uses film, which you have to buy in small rolls, and you cannot see the picture until it has been developed.

I took it to a photography shop in town, where an old man showed me how to load the film. 'Think before you press the button,' he told me. 'You only have thirty-six pictures, so each one must count.' That was very different from my phone, on which I take hundreds of pictures a day and delete most of them.

I spent a week photographing my street, my friends and my little brother. When I collected the pictures, I was surprised. Some were blurry, and one was only a finger, but several were beautiful, with soft colours that no phone could give. My mother cried when she saw a photograph of our dog sleeping, because it looked just like an old family picture.

Now I carry the camera everywhere. I take fewer pictures than before, but I look at the world more carefully, and I feel closer to my grandmother.

options: It was far too expensive for her
It had belonged to a stranger
questions.explanation: It is a heavy metal camera from the 1970s that uses film.

options: To buy a lot more film to practise

questions.explanation: The film allowed only thirty-six pictures, while the phone takes hundreds.

questions.explanation: The photograph of the sleeping dog looked just like an old family picture.

options: She prefers using her phone again now
She looks at things more carefully
She is bored with photography by now
questions.explanation: She takes fewer pictures but looks at the world more carefully.

parts.title: Taking better photographs
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
Many people think that you need an expensive camera to take good photographs, but this is not true. [1] The following tips will help you take better pictures with any camera, even a phone.

First, think about the light. The best time to take photographs is early in the morning or just before sunset, when the light is soft and golden. [2] In the middle of the day, the sun is high and can make faces look hard and shadowy.

Second, get closer to your subject. Beginners often stand too far away, so the person looks tiny. [3] If you are photographing a friend, try to fill the picture with their face.

Third, look at the background before you press the button. [4] A tree growing out of someone's head is one of the most common mistakes! Moving one step to the side can solve the problem.

Finally, do not be afraid to take many photographs. [5] Nobody becomes an expert without making mistakes, so keep practising.
sentences: Many beautiful pictures are taken with very simple cameras.
My brother likes to take photographs of birds.
Sometimes there is something strange behind your subject.
Photographs taken then often look warm and magical.
Do not forget to charge your phone before you go out.
You can always delete the ones that you do not like.
This makes the details clearer and the picture more interesting.
Flash makes faces look flat and white.

gaps.explanation: "This is not true" is followed by evidence that simple cameras can produce beautiful pictures.
"Taken then" refers to early morning or sunset, when the light is soft and golden.
"This" refers to getting closer, which shows details; the example with a friend's face follows.
The strange thing behind the subject leads to the example of a tree growing out of a head.
"The ones you do not like" refers to the many photographs that you take.

parts.title: A photography workshop
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: sylvester
turns.text: Hello, everyone, and welcome to today’s photography workshop. My name is Sylvester. We will start at the park gate at ten o’clock and finish at one. Please don’t come at nine, because nobody will be here and the gate is locked. First, I’ll show you how to hold your camera, because most beginners take blurry pictures. Many people hold it with one hand, like a phone, but you should use both hands and keep your elbows close to your body. Next, the subject. We are going to walk to the lake. Many of you will want to photograph the ducks and the boats, and you can do that at the end, but for the first exercise I want you to photograph flowers. They stay still, and they teach you about light. Now, the competition. At the end of the day, I’ll choose the best picture. The winner doesn’t get a camera, I’m afraid, but a book about photography, with beautiful pictures by famous photographers. Next, money. The workshop costs fifteen pounds for each person. It was twenty last year, but our new sponsor helps us. Members of the photo club pay only ten, but only if they show their card, so please find it now. Finally, the walk. The path around the lake is five kilometres long, but we won’t do all of it. We will walk about three kilometres and stop often to take pictures. Please wear comfortable shoes, and bring water and a hat in case it’s sunny. If you have a tripod, bring it, but it isn’t necessary. I will also give you a printed map of the park at the gate, and a list of the rules for taking photos near the water. Please keep it with you all day. Are there any questions before we start?

gaps.explanation: Ducks and boats are for the end; first they photograph flowers.

It was twenty last year and club members pay ten; the normal price is fifteen.

parts.title: A travel photographer
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: roisin
turns.text: Marlon, how did you pay for your first camera?

turns.speaker: marlon
turns.text: My parents wanted to buy it, but I said no, I wanted to earn it myself. I won a school competition once, but the prize was a book, so that didn’t help. At thirteen I delivered newspapers every morning for eight months, in rain and in snow, and I saved everything. When I finally bought that camera, I felt really proud.

turns.speaker: roisin
turns.text: You had a problem in Peru. How did you feel?

turns.speaker: marlon
turns.text: People think I lost my passport and my money, or that my camera was stolen, because those things happen to travellers. No, I slipped on a rock and the camera fell into the river. Strangely, I was calm, because I had saved the pictures that morning. The camera was expensive, but I wasn’t worried about the money. My guide felt terrible, and I wasn’t angry with him at all, it was my fault, and I laughed about it that evening.

turns.speaker: roisin
turns.text: Why do you like photographing Iceland?

turns.speaker: marlon
turns.text: It isn’t cheap, honestly, tourists spend a fortune there. And the people are friendly, but they are friendly in other countries too. What I love is the light. It changes every minute: clear blue, then grey cloud, then orange. You never take the same photo twice, and that keeps me interested after so many visits. I’ve been four times.

turns.speaker: roisin
turns.text: What makes a good photograph?

turns.speaker: marlon
turns.text: A famous place isn’t enough. You see those pictures everywhere, and they’re boring. Colour is nice, but black and white can be wonderful too. A good photograph tells a story. When you look at it, you ask: who is this person, and what happens next? That’s the difference between a postcard and a real picture.

turns.speaker: roisin
turns.text: What advice do you give beginners?

turns.speaker: marlon
turns.text: Don’t buy expensive equipment. My first camera was cheap, and I learned more with it. Don’t photograph only people either, try everything. My best advice is to print your photographs. On a screen you see them for two seconds, but on a wall you notice the details and the mistakes.

turns.speaker: roisin
turns.text: What are you planning for next year?

turns.speaker: marlon
turns.text: A book about Peru is an idea, my publisher asks me every month, but I’m not ready. Teaching abroad sounds nice, but I’d miss my own work. What’s certain is an exhibition in London in May. I’m excited, and a little nervous, to be honest. Fifty of my photographs will be on the wall, and I still have to choose them.

questions.explanation: He says that expensive equipment is not necessary and people are not the only subject; he advises printing photographs.

questions.prompt: What is he planning for next year?
options: A book about his time in Peru
A new job as a teacher abroad
questions.explanation: The book and the teaching job are only ideas; the exhibition in London in May is certain.

parts.title: Getting to know you
parts.instructions: Answer each question in your own words. Aim to speak for 20-30 seconds.

questions.prompt: Do you like taking photographs? What do you usually photograph?
Do you prefer looking at photos on a screen or printed on paper?
Tell me about a photograph that is special to you.
Would you like to be a professional photographer? Why or why not?

parts.title: Describe a photograph
parts.instructions: Look at the photograph and speak for about one minute. Describe what you can see and say what the person might be feeling.
parts.prompt: A person taking a photograph of white roses.
